strengths: Compelling and impactful application bridging precision oncology, multi-omics data integration, knowledge graph reasoning, and large language models.

Well-structured framework combining initial language reasoning, step-wise RL subgraph generation supervised by a pretrained GNN (GPRM) and domain rule checks, followed by final graph-grounded answer generation.

Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse cancer cohorts, unseen holdout cancer types, external validation on pediatric cancer datasets (PedDep), and thorough ablations on graph/reward components.
Meaningful biological validation, including functional pathway enrichment analysis (WikiPathways, GAD) and expert bioinformatician evaluation of the generated subgraphs for mechanistic plausibility.
weaknesses: Relatively small dataset scale: Target-QA comprises only 363 annotated cancer cell line instances (300 train / 63 test), which is modest for training multi-component pipelines involving LLM fine-tuning and RL policy optimization.

While Hit@5/10 and Jaccard show noticeable improvements, the overall gains in Precision and Recall over strong task-finetuned baselines (e.g., L3-FT(QA)+Omics) are relatively incremental (precision goes from ~0.525 to ~0.547).

Formulating target discovery as an autoregressive text generation problem requiring downstream NER extraction seems somewhat unnatural compared to standard graph ranking or link prediction formulations, given that the target set is evaluated purely as an unordered entity set.
Occasional terminology anomalies in the text, such as references to 'ChatGPT 5.1' / 'ChatGPT-5' (in Appendix A, Section D.3, and Table 15), which appear to be typos or non-standard version labels.

strengths: Compelling and clinically meaningful problem formulation: The paper tackles a significant challenge in precision medicine—predicting CRISPR-mediated gene essentiality/vulnerabilities from patient-specific multi-omic profiles while generating biologically grounded, interpretable subgraphs.

Well-structured framework coupling GNNs and LLMs: Using a reinforcement learning generator guided by a Graph Process Reward Model (GPRM)—combining biological plausibility/schema validity, rollout simulations, and oncogenicity classification—provides an elegant way to generate task-relevant subgraphs without requiring ground-truth reasoning path annotations.

Comprehensive biological and qualitative validation: Beyond standard retrieval/ranking metrics, the paper provides extensive validation of the generated subgraphs via pathway enrichment analysis (WikiPathways, KEGG, GAD), human expert evaluations by bioinformaticians, and LLM-as-a-judge scoring.

Extensive ablations and generalization experiments: The authors conduct thoughtful ablation studies examining reward density, individual reward components, omics/KG perturbations, held-out cancer types, and zero-shot transfer to an external pediatric cancer dataset (PedDep).
weaknesses: Limited dataset size for the Target-QA benchmark: The benchmark comprises only 363 cancer cell line samples in total (300 train, 63 test) split across more than 20 TCGA cancer types. This results in just 2 to 7 test instances per cancer type (e.g., only 2 samples for HNSC, LUSC, and STAD; 3 for GBM, SARC, OV, SKCM), which increases metric variance and limits the statistical robustness of per-cohort claims.

Modest performance margin over the fine-tuned LLM baseline: Across overall metrics, the fine-tuned LLM baseline (L3-FT(QA) + Omics) already achieves a Precision of 0.5250 and F1 of 0.5094, while the full GALAX model achieves 0.5472 Precision and 0.5399 F1. In several individual cancer cohorts (e.g., Table 39 for KIRC and Table 43 for PRAD), graph-retrieval baselines like RoG and GNN-RAG outperform GALAX.

Clarity and discrepancies regarding model versions: The text references 'ChatGPT 5.1' and 'ChatGPT-5' as writing assistants / baseline path generators (e.g., in Section 2, Section D.3, Section E.2, and Appendix A), which appear to be typos or confusing naming conventions for existing OpenAI models (e.g., GPT-4o). Clarification on exact model versions and API endpoints used is needed for reproducibility.

Evaluation protocol details: Predicting 100 targets via free-form text generation and subsequently parsing them via GPT-4o-mini NER introduces potential parsing inconsistencies and dependency on external commercial APIs for evaluation. A standardized ranked retrieval or classification evaluation over candidate gene sets would ensure higher reproducibility and benchmark standardization.

strengths: The ambition to integrate multi-omics features, biological knowledge graphs, and large language models for precision oncology target identification addresses an important problem.
The paper provides an extensive appendix with cohort-level breakdowns across numerous TCGA cancer types and enrichment analyses.
The pipeline combines multiple complementary components, including graph pretraining, reinforcement learning with rule-based gating, and LLM finetuning.
weaknesses: Severe benchmark design flaw regarding pan-essential genes: In the DepMap CRISPR screening data, a substantial fraction of the top-100 dependencies in any given cell line are pan-cancer common essential genes (e.g., core ribosomal, proteasomal, and spliceosomal components such as RPS18, SF3A3, SNRPF shown in Figure 1). The benchmark does not filter out common essential genes to evaluate selective/context-specific dependencies. Consequently, any model finetuned on Target-QA (L3-FT(QA)) jumps from ~0.01 to ~0.51 F1 simply by memorizing the ubiquitous pan-essential gene set, while the complex RL and graph-reasoning modules in GALAX provide only an incremental ~3% gain over standard finetuning.

Conceptual mismatch in the reward formulation: The graph classifier g(·) used as the process reward is trained as a binary classifier distinguishing cancerous vs. non-cancerous cell lines (on only 297 cancer and 39 non-cancer samples). Rewarding a subgraph based on whether it predicts general oncogenicity does not logically equate to scoring whether knocking out a specific gene in that pathway induces synthetic lethality or cell death in a patient-specific manner.

Fictitious model references and evaluation artifacts: In Section 5, Appendix D.4, and Appendix E.2 (Table 15), the authors claim to employ 'ChatGPT 5.1' for generating baseline reasoning paths and 'ChatGPT-5.1' and 'Gemini-3.0 Pro' as automated LLM judges (m1, m2), and Appendix A mentions using 'ChatGPT-5'. These models do not exist, raising critical concerns regarding the integrity, reproducibility, and validity of the reported experimental evaluations.

Extremely limited dataset scale: Target-QA contains only 363 cell lines in total (300 train, 63 test), which is very small for training a multi-stage framework involving GNN pretraining, reinforcement learning policies, and LLM finetuning.

Marginal gain over trivial baselines: The paper lacks essential baselines, such as a static frequency prior (predicting the most common top-100 essential genes across the training cohort). Given the high overlap of pan-essential genes, such a naive baseline would likely match or exceed the performance of the non-graph LLM finetuning.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant challenge in computational oncology: integrating high-dimensional multi-omic profiles, topological interaction networks, and biomedical text for therapeutic target prioritization.

The proposed framework introduces an interesting conceptual idea of using a GNN-based proxy reward model to guide step-wise sub-network generation for LLM reasoning without requiring step-by-step human annotations.
The authors conduct extensive per-cancer-type evaluations across multiple TCGA cohorts and provide biological pathway enrichment analyses (e.g., WikiPathways, DAVID) for generated subgraphs.
weaknesses: Flawed task formulation and misleading baseline comparisons: The Target-QA task requires an LLM to generate a textual list of 100 CRISPR essential gene symbols. Non-finetuned LLMs, M2T, and traditional GAT baselines achieve near-zero performance (Precision/Recall ~ 0.001) primarily because they are not trained to output the exact requested list format or memorized gene candidate distributions. The performance leap is almost entirely attributable to standard supervised fine-tuning on the Target-QA data (L3-FT(QA) jumps from ~0.01 to 0.52 F1), whereas the proposed RL subgraph module yields only marginal incremental gains (~2%), even underperforming L3-FT(QA) in several cancer subtypes (e.g., Medulloblastoma, Prostate Adenocarcinoma, Stomach Adenocarcinoma).

Disconnect in reward formulation: The Graph Process Reward Model (GPRM) relies on a GNN classifier trained on a binary classification objective (cancerous vs. non-cancerous, |O|=2). It is conceptually ungrounded why optimizing a subgraph to maximize the probability of being labeled 'cancerous' would specifically guide the identification of cell-line-specific synthetic lethal or essential gene targets.

Extremely limited dataset size: The Target-QA dataset consists of only 363 cell lines (300 training, 63 testing) partitioned across more than a dozen cancer types, resulting in evaluation sets with only 2 to 7 samples per cancer cohort. This limited sample size makes the evaluation susceptible to high variance and questions the statistical reliability of the reported results.

Writing and presentation issues: The manuscript contains multiple rough edges, including blank URL footnotes (Footnotes 1, 2, 4, 5, 6), glaring duplications (e.g., Page 2: 'especially when the input context becomes large and complex, and and to respect biological topology at scale when the input context becomes large and complex'), grammatical glitches ('has has', 'ratiofor'), and misspelled figure titles (e.g., 'Initial langugage answering training loss' in Figures 8 and 10).

strengths: Ambitious goal of bridging quantitative multi-omics, structured biological knowledge graphs, and large language models for target prioritization.
The paper attempts to tackle mechanistic interpretability by having an explicit graph generation step rather than treating LLM reasoning as an ungrounded black box.
Comprehensive reporting of per-cancer cohort metrics and biological enrichment analyses (pathway and disease terms) for representative cell lines.
weaknesses: Absence of critical naive/frequency baselines: In genome-wide CRISPR screens (such as DepMap), a significant proportion of top dependency genes are pan-cancer common essentials (e.g., core ribosomal, proteasomal, and spliceosomal genes such as RPL12, RPS18, PSMA3, and SF3A3, several of which appear in the paper's own examples). The paper lacks a standard baseline that simply predicts the top 100 most frequent essential genes across the training set. Without this comparison, it is impossible to verify whether the ~50% precision/recall comes from true cell-specific mechanistic reasoning or trivial memorization of general essential genes.

Marginal and inconsistent gains from the RL/PRM framework: Ablation results in Tables 1 and 2 reveal that nearly all performance is gained simply by supervised fine-tuning of LLaMA-3 on the Target-QA data (jumping from ~0.002 to ~0.509 F1). The full RL-guided subgraph generation (GALAX) yields only a modest incremental boost overall (~0.540 F1) and is inconsistent across cohorts, performing noticeably worse than the simple SFT baseline `L3-FT(QA)` on several cancer types (e.g., PRAD in Table 35, STAD in Table 21, and MB in Table 22).

Flawed reward model design: The GPRM uses the output of a GNN binary classifier trained to distinguish cancerous vs. non-cancerous samples on a tiny set of 336 cell lines. Using a binary cancer classification score as an intermediate step-wise reward to guide the assembly of specific CRISPR vulnerability networks lacks biological grounding and risks severe reward hacking, as global oncogenicity classification does not imply gene knockout sensitivity.

Very small sample size and underpowered evaluation: The Target-QA dataset consists of only 363 cell lines in total (300 train, 63 test). When broken down across cancer types, many test sets contain only 2 to 4 cell lines (e.g., 2 in HNSC, 3 in GBM, 3 in SARC). Reporting precision, recall, and Hit@k on such minuscule test subsets introduces extreme variance and undermines statistical significance.

Ad-hoc training procedure and reproducibility gaps: The RL policy optimization relies on heuristic retry loops with dynamically changing hyperparameters (e.g., varying learning rates by epoch multipliers, manually reducing max nodes and step counts) rather than a stable, principled RL algorithm. Additionally, several footnotes (Footnotes 1, 2, 4, 5, 6) and citations (e.g., 'Luo et al.;' on page 2) are incomplete or empty, and repetitive text errors appear in the main draft (e.g., page 2 duplication: 'especially when the input context becomes large and complex...').

strengths: The paper tackles a challenging and impactful problem in precision oncology: integrating multi-modal omic features, structured biomedical knowledge graphs, and LLM reasoning to prioritize CRISPR-based therapeutic targets.

The formulation of subgraph reasoning via reinforcement learning supervised by a pretrained Graph Neural Network (serving as a Graph Process Reward Model) is an interesting and creative direction to circumvent the lack of stepwise reasoning annotations.

The authors conduct detailed biological validation and pathway enrichment analysis (e.g., WikiPathways, GAD) on individual cancer cell lines, providing qualitative evidence that the constructed subgraphs capture established oncogenic pathways.
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is critically small: The Target-QA benchmark comprises only 363 cell-line samples in total (300 training, 63 testing). When stratified across 20+ cancer types, individual cancer cohorts have as few as 1 to 3 test samples (e.g., HNSC, LUSC, STAD have 2 test samples each; several others have 1), making per-cohort metrics and statistical conclusions highly susceptible to sample variance.

Marginal empirical gain over standard fine-tuning: The vast majority of the performance improvement comes from supervised fine-tuning of the base LLM on Target-QA (jumping from ~0.007 precision to ~0.525), whereas the entire RL-guided subgraph generation pipeline adds only an incremental improvement (~0.525 to ~0.547 in precision). Moreover, in multiple cancer types in the appendix tables (e.g., PRAD, LAML, STAD), standard fine-tuning matches or outperforms GALAX.

Conceptual disconnect in the reward function: The GNN reward model is trained on a binary classification objective (cancerous vs. non-cancerous status / disease classification). It is conceptually unclear why maximizing disease classification probability directly aligns with CRISPR knockout vulnerability/essentiality, as genetic dependencies often involve synthetic lethality or specific signaling choke points rather than simple disease predictors.

Clarity and presentation issues: Several placeholder footnote links are left blank (Footnotes 1, 2, 4, and 5 contain empty 'GitHub:' and 'Hugging Face:'). There are multiple typographical errors (e.g., duplicated words like 'and and' on page 2, 'ratiofor' on page 15, 'trasnscription' and 'geomic' on page 15, 'langugage' in Figure 8/10 captions), and several figures (such as the radar plots in Figures 4a and 11) have illegible text due to low resolution/scaling.
